4% rule of thumb (Bengen, 1994) -- a rule of thumb, not a guarantee. Math: $107,269 x 4% = $4,291/yr = about $358/month

alt_titles: Your Dad Retired at 62. Why Can't You?
Who Moved Your Retirement Finish Line?
youtube.hook: Dave's retirement calculator says 70 -- five years longer than his dad. Who moved the finish line? And what's the one boring line quietly stealing years? Dave types his savings into a retirement calculator and it says he'll work until 70 -- five extra years compared to his dad who stopped at 62. We follow the whole story: how Dad had a pension (a vending machine that never runs out) but Dave got a 401(k) lunchbox he has to fill himself and make last; how the Social Security finish line quietly moved from 65 to 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later; what the typical 401(k) balance is for people aged 55-64 (about $107,000, which gives roughly $358/month); how the risk moved from employers onto workers; why Dave's backup plan 'just work until 70' isn't a plan (46% of retirees stop earlier than planned due to health or company changes); and the one boring line in Dave's account -- the expense ratio -- that could cost him $64,000 over 35 years (DOL example: 1.5% vs 0.5% fees). Then how Dave fights back: grabbing the full match, learning the Social Security 62/67/70 dial, and checking that boring line.
